text: Governments should regulate social media because the platforms profit from engagement even when it harms users. The 2019 FTC settlement, where Facebook paid $5 billion over privacy violations, shows that companies do not fix problems until forced to. Regulation should focus on data practices and transparency about algorithms, not on deciding which opinions are allowed. Without that outside pressure, the same violations keep repeating.

Governments should not regulate social media content, because whoever holds power would decide what counts as harmful. Countries that already censor online speech show how easily rules meant to stop misinformation are used against critics. Platforms can improve their own moderation, and users can choose to leave. The risk of state control outweighs the benefits.

The EU's Digital Services Act, adopted in 2022, is a useful model, and other governments should adopt similar rules requiring platforms to explain how their recommendation systems work. Under this law large platforms must assess risks such as the spread of illegal content. Critics say it could burden small companies, but the law applies its strictest duties only to the biggest platforms.

Governments should set a minimum age for social media accounts, because children are especially vulnerable to addictive design. Australia passed a law in 2024 banning under-16s from holding accounts, which shows this is a workable policy, though it is too early to know how well it will be enforced. Parents alone cannot compete with apps designed by teams of engineers to keep children scrolling.

Social media companies should be treated like public utilities and regulated accordingly, because a few firms now control how billions of people get news and talk to each other. Their size gives them power no private company should hold without oversight. This is why competition rules and transparency requirements are necessary.

In 2018 it was revealed that Cambridge Analytica had harvested data from tens of millions of Facebook profiles without proper consent. Facebook was later fined heavily by regulators, including a $5 billion penalty from the US FTC. These events happened because the platform's data controls were weak.

I believe governments must regulate social media because misinformation spreads faster than corrections. During elections false stories can reach huge audiences before anyone checks them. Studies have shown that false news travels further than true news online, so platforms should be legally required to slow down the spread of viral claims.
